own_scenes.desc: Tras Let’s Get It On, «Me and Mrs. Jones» de Billy Paul y «Let’s Stay Together» de Al Green llegó una nueva hornada de cantantes sensuales. Barry White, con su orquesta de estudio sobre una sección rítmica de R&B, unió la elegancia occidental y la sensualidad negra: un lujo negro impensable diez años antes. Los Moments («Sexy Mama»), Main Ingredient, los Miracles («Do It Baby»), Leon Haywood («I Want’a Do Something Freaky to You», base de «Nothin’ but a G Thang» de Dr. Dre) o New Birth mezclaron psicodelia, melodía y funk sucio; Sylvia Robinson susurró «Pillow Talk» (1973) y Major Harris remató «Love Won’t Let Me Wait» con un orgasmo simulado.

refs.q: Los Angeles producer Barry White brought his huge frame and deep, low voice to dark bedroom musings
refs.para: On the heels of “Let’s Get It On” and other lush yet down-to-earth soul arrangements like Billy Paul’s exquisite “Me and Mrs. Jones,” and Al Green’s funky pop breakthrough “Let’s Stay Together” in 1971, a new breed of sultry soul crooners hit the scene. Los Angeles producer Barry White brought his huge frame and deep, low voice to dark bedroom musings that captured the nation’s imagination, and scored consecutive pop Top 10 sweet funk sides in 1973 with “I’m Gonna Love You Just a Little More, Baby” and “Never Gonna Give You Up.” Using a vast collection of studio musicians he dubbed an orchestra along with a standard R&B rhythm section, White’s plush layers and grooving, soulful swinging brought about an incredible synthesis—Western elegance with breathy black sexiness. White had found a new level of black luxury—a lifestyle never even considered ten years earlier.
